title: Condensate loss estimation and transient solar-to-vapor conversion efficiency for effective performance evaluation of the inclined solar still
author: Abimbola, Takaijudin, et al.

steps.title: Define condensation surface geometry
steps.instruction: Identify each condensation surface (CSi) on the glass cover, record its shape, and calculate its total area (CS1, CS2, …, CSn) using appropriate geometric formulas.

steps.title: Calculate loss area per surface
steps.instruction: For each surface, determine the portion below the condensate collection channel (∂CSi) that contributes to loss, and compute its area based on the channel‑slope geometry.

steps.title: Compute loss fractions
steps.instruction: Calculate the loss fraction for each surface as ∂CSi/CSi. Then obtain the overall condensate loss fraction δloss = ( Σ ∂CSi ) / ( Σ CSi ). For the prototype described, δloss = 18.5 % (Eq 1).

steps.title: Measure experimental condensate yield
steps.instruction: Run the solar still in passive mode under direct insolation. Collect condensate hourly from 09:00 to 16:00 for three consecutive days. Record hourly distillate yield ṁ (ml m⁻²) and cumulative yield m (ml m⁻²). Example cumulative average yield = 3842.2 ml m⁻²; cumulative experimentally recovered loss = 657.9 ml m⁻².

steps.title: Calculate total recoverable condensate
steps.instruction: Using the measured cumulative condensate m and the overall loss fraction δloss, compute total recoverable condensate Q = m / (1 − δloss) (Eq 2). For the example, Q ≈ 3842.2 / 0.815 = 4715 ml m⁻² (rounded to the reported 4711.1 ml m⁻²).

steps.title: Determine actual condensate loss
steps.instruction: Compute the actual loss mloss = Q × δloss (Eq 3). For the example, mloss = 832.6 ml m⁻².

steps.title: Record hourly temperature and irradiance
steps.instruction: For each productivity hour, measure water temperature Twi (°C) and solar irradiance I(t) (W m⁻²). Also note the basin surface area As (m²).

steps.title: Calculate latent heat per hour
steps.instruction: For each hour, calculate the latent heat of vaporization hfg using Eq 7: hfg = 2.493×10⁶ [1 − (9.4479×10⁻⁴ Twi + 1.3132×10⁻⁷ Twi² − 4.794×10⁻⁹ Twi³)] (J kg⁻¹). Convert to kJ kg⁻¹ as shown in Table 3.

steps.title: Compute transient efficiency
steps.instruction: For each hour, compute the transient solar‑to‑vapor efficiency ηsv‑trans = (ṁ × hfg) / (As × I(t)) (Eq 6). Use ṁ in kg m⁻² (convert from ml m⁻² by dividing by 1000), hfg in J kg⁻¹, As in m², and I(t) in W m⁻². Record η (%) for each hour.

steps.title: Calculate average daily efficiency
steps.instruction: Average the hourly efficiencies using Eq 8: X̄η = ( Σ ηsv‑trans ) / n, where n is the number of productivity hours. For the data set, mean hourly transient efficiency = 113.4 % (variation coefficient 0.0225). Using conventional daily‑average values gives ηsv = 108.4 %.

steps.title: Summarize geometric loss data
steps.instruction: Record the surface‑area and loss‑area data for each condensation surface as follows: Surface 1 – area 1156 cm², loss area 270 cm², loss % = 17.39 %, contribution % = 9.72 %; Surface 2 – area 6000 cm², loss area 1300 cm², loss % = 21.74 %, contribution % = 6.53 %; Surface 3 – area 1560 cm², loss area 627.9 cm², loss % = 40.22 %, contribution % = 2.44 %; Surface 4 – area 6000 cm², loss area 600 cm², loss % = 10.00 %, contribution % = 1.40 %. Overall δloss = 18.5 % (Eq 1).

steps.title: Report yield with loss inclusion
steps.instruction: Compare conventional yield with loss‑included yield. Highest hourly recovered yield = 869.1 ml m⁻² (12:00‑13:00); after adding estimated loss it becomes 1066.4 ml m⁻². Cumulative recovered yield = 4711.1 ml m⁻²; after adding loss factor it becomes 5780.5 ml m⁻².

description: In evaluating the performance of the solar still, losses in condensate due to the condensate collection channel slope in the double slope solar still were not accounted for. Similarly, the solar-to-vapor conversion efficiencies were only evaluated based on the daily average temperature values, rather than based on the transient hourly average temperature. These two limitations suggest that the conventional methods for the performance evaluation of the solar still, regarding the freshwater productivity and the solar-to-vapor conversion efficiency, do not entirely indicate the actual output of the device. Therefore, in this study, we propose two considerations for a more comprehensive performance evaluation of the double-slope inclined solar still. The first consideration is a geometrical method to factor-in the condensate loss in the overall distillate productivity, while the other is the use of the actual transient hourly temperature values for the evaluation of the solar-to-vapor conversion efficiency as a replacement for the fixed daily average temperature—thus, giving rise to a transient solar-to-vapor conversion efficiency. Although these two considerations aim at improving the overall method of evaluating the performance of the solar still, the condensate loss estimation targets to account for the unrecovered condensate during solar still experiments owing to the slope of the condensate channel, while the transient solar-to-vapor conversion efficiency approach targets to simplify the efficiency of the solar still on hourly basis rather than on usual daily basis. To validate the two considerations, the condensate loss on a double-slope solar still prototype was calculated geometrically and compared with the actual experimental losses, while on the other hand, the average solar-to-vapour conversion efficiency computed both on the daily and the hourly bases were also compared.1.A geometrical method for condensate loss estimation In the double-slope inclined solar
